problems.description: test_app.py has module-level constants that should be UPPER_CASE per the convention scan (score 0.91, 1 violation)

Mixes threading.Lock into an asyncio server; currently safe because the lock only guards synchronous dict access, but the dual concurrency model is fragile if any await is ever introduced inside the locked region
_broadcast fans out one asyncio task per client with no backpressure or per-client queue; a slow/hung client could accumulate pending sends under load

strengths: Greenfield WebSocket server keeps the event loop free of blocking I/O and uses asyncio idioms (create_task, gather with return_exceptions) correctly
ClientRegistry cleanly encapsulates connection state behind a lock with a well-scoped public API (add/remove/count/get_all)
SonarQube delta is clean: 0 bugs, 0 smells, 0 complexity increase, 0 duplication across +322/-252 lines
Robust handling of closed/stale sockets during broadcast via return_exceptions=True rather than crashing the loop
commit_reviews.summary: A clean, zero-smell greenfield WebSocket implementation that respects Python/async conventions (0.91 score) but swaps the prior modular Flask structure wholesale, with only minor concurrency-model and naming nits.

problems.description: _broadcast_to_channel calls registry.get_all() (full client dict) to resolve only a handful of subscriber sockets; could look up subscribers directly without copying the entire registry.
subscribe/unsubscribe with a missing or empty 'channel' field silently no-ops with no error ack to the client, unlike the explicit confirmations sent on success.
/channels/{name}/subscribers parsing relies on positional split (parts[3] == 'subscribers'), which is fragile to path-shape changes; a length/prefix check would be more robust.
test_app.py introduces module-level constants that should be UPPER_CASE (per the 0.91 convention score and SonarQube finding).

strengths: Channel registry methods mirror the existing add/remove pattern: lock-protected, with empty-channel cleanup on unsubscribe and client removal to prevent leaks.
_broadcast_to_channel parallels the existing _broadcast/direct dispatch, keeping handler control flow consistent with established conventions.
Comprehensive async tests cover subscription confirmations, channel broadcast, and teardown cleanup.
No new imports or file-level restructuring; feature slots cleanly into the existing app.py registry architecture.
commit_reviews.summary: Clean, pattern-consistent pub/sub extension that respects the existing registry and broadcast idioms with solid test coverage; only minor robustness and naming nits.

problems.description: channel "ws:broadcast:all" is subscribed both explicitly (subscribe) and via the "ws:broadcast:*" pattern (psubscribe), so all-grace broadcasts are delivered twice; the guard `if channel == "ws:broadcast:*": continue` is dead code because pmessage "channel" is the actual channel, not the matched pattern
every broadcast/send/direct path performs an inline awaited db.commit() (SQLite fsync) before returning, serializing a disk write into the hot broadcast path
_send_direct persists rows with channel=None while _broadcast_to_channel preserves the channel, so the persisted history is inconsistent for direct sends
test_app.py module-level constants are lowercase instead of UPPER_CASE (per SonarQube convention measurement)

strengths: Clean background lifecycle: _start_background/_stop_background with task cancel and resource teardown (Redis + DB) on shutdown
Lazy singleton init for Redis and SQLite keeps module-level state explicit and testable
Refactor preserves the existing _broadcast/_broadcast_to_channel/_send_direct signatures and retains the local delivery path, so callers are unaffected
Measured zero bugs and zero duplications with +13 functions and +7 imports added cleanly
commit_reviews.summary: Solid Redis pub/sub + SQLite persistence integration that preserves existing APIs and lifecycle hygiene, but the overlapping subscribe/psubscribe on ws:broadcast:all risks duplicate delivery and the per-message inline db.commit() adds avoidable hot-path cost.

problems.description: NotificationServer.handle_message grew +5 cognitive complexity via nested if/elif dispatch (subscribe/unsubscribe/direct/broadcast); a dispatch table would scale better as message types accumulate.
_get_transport() factory requires manual modification for each new TRANSPORT type; a registry/dict lookup would make the seam extensible without touching the factory.
BaseTransport.on_connect's `connection` parameter is untyped while sibling abstract methods carry full type hints; inconsistent with the module's snake_case/typed style.
The measured convention violation (module-level constant casing) is in test_app.py, but the diff only touches app.py — the violation appears pre-existing and unrelated to this commit.

strengths: Centralizes previously duplicated broadcast/channel/direct send logic (json.dumps + asyncio.gather) into a single transport abstraction, cutting ~105 lines with 0.0% duplications.
Respects existing module patterns: module-level singletons (_transport alongside _redis/_db), async task usage, and registry delegation.
Preserves prior behavior parity, including exception-tolerant sends and return_exceptions=True gathers.
Clean ABC seam (BaseTransport) with a concrete WebSocketTransport and no new dependencies (+1 import only).
commit_reviews.summary: A clean, pattern-consistent transport abstraction that removes real duplication and adds no bugs or dependencies, with only modest cognitive-complexity growth and a rigid factory as minor follow-ups.

problems.description: Only rate limiting is tested; the /history endpoint and message TTL expiry loop — two of the three features added — have no coverage.
_stop_background reassigns module-level constants RATE_LIMIT/MESSAGE_TTL_DAYS from env on shutdown; mutating 'constants' is an anti-pattern and the re-read has no meaningful runtime effect.
The /history handler largely duplicates the /messages query/parse/serialize logic (+3.5% duplication, +28 cognitive complexity); a shared row-to-message helper would remove it.

Rate limiting is enforced in the transport handler() rather than NotificationServer.handle_message, splitting a cross-cutting concern across layers; _check_rate_limit calls _init_redis() with no outage fallback, so a Redis failure raises out of the connection loop.
New rate-limit error uses payload {"error": true, "message": ...} while the codebase's existing errors use a string under "error" (e.g. {"error": "invalid message"}), an inconsistent error shape.
test_app.py has module-level constants that should be UPPER_CASE (measured by SonarQube; the only convention violation).

strengths: Features integrate cleanly with the existing architecture: Redis for the rate-limit counter, SQLite for TTL deletion, and a system-message response consistent with the transport pattern
Config exposed as UPPER_CASE env-backed constants (RATE_LIMIT, MESSAGE_TTL_DAYS) consistent with REDIS_URL/DATABASE_URL
Background expiry task wired into _start_background/_stop_background with proper cancel-and-await teardown, mirroring the existing _listener_task lifecycle
Parameterized SQL everywhere (no injection); limit+1 sentinel correctly implements has_more pagination
Rate-limit behavior is well tested via the app-module attribute seam
commit_reviews.summary: Well-tested, convention-compliant cross-cutting additions that respect the existing module-global architecture, but the duplicated /history query logic, +28 complexity, constant mutation in _stop_background, and untested /history and TTL paths make it a net maintainability regression.

compounding_issues: Session 1's in-memory ClientRegistry + module-global singletons (_redis, _db, _transport, _listener_task) forced every later session to layer on top of mutable global state; session 3's Redis integration had to bolt a pub/sub listener onto that design, so connection state was never distributed — cross-instance delivery only covers messages, not registry/sync

Single-file monolith persisted to the end (app.py 139 -> 560 lines); session 4's 'refactor' stayed within one file and left module-level functions (_broadcast, _save_message, process_request, handler) mixed with the new class abstractions — a half-applied decomposition
Session 3 introduced a hard Redis infra dependency mid-story; the headline multi-instance delivery feature is only tested against fakeredis, so real distributed behavior was never exercised
Session 5 had to hack _stop_background to re-read env vars into module globals (RATE_LIMIT, MESSAGE_TTL_DAYS) just to keep tests isolated from the global-singleton design

Committed __pycache__ .pyc binaries in every session commit; session 5's session log records a stale '40 passed' run even though the committed test file holds 53 tests (the final state is green at 53, verified independently)
The seed codebase (Flask auth API) was domain-mismatched to the notification_service story and fully discarded in session 1's greenfield rewrite, contributing nothing to the build
key_decisions: Session 1: greenfield pivot from the Flask auth seed to an asyncio/websockets real-time server with a thread-safe in-memory ClientRegistry as the connection store
Session 2: topic-based channel subscription model (subscribe/unsubscribe, channel-targeted routing, /channels HTTP introspection) layered onto the registry
Session 3: Redis pub/sub backbone (ws:broadcast:all / ws:broadcast:{channel} / ws:direct:{client_id}) for cross-instance delivery plus aiosqlite message persistence with a /messages history endpoint
Session 4: transport abstraction — BaseTransport ABC + WebSocketTransport + NotificationServer, decoupling protocol I/O from core routing behind a TRANSPORT env factory

Session 5: production hardening — Redis-based per-client rate limiting, message TTL retention with a background hourly expiry loop, and a /history endpoint with limit/channel/since filters and has_more pagination
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved monotonically across the five sessions, with tests passing and growing at every checkpoint (12 -> 31 -> 40 -> 40 -> 53). Session 1 delivered a minimal but functional WebSocket server; session 2 added a clean channel/subscription layer; session 3 was the largest leap, wiring Redis pub/sub and SQLite persistence with strong integration tests; session 4 was a net-neutral refactor that introduced a transport abstraction while keeping behavior identical and all 40 tests green; session 5 capped the arc with real production hardening (rate limiting, message TTL expiry, filtered/paginated history) finishing at 53 passing tests. The only flat patch is the refactor session, which changed structure without adding behavior, but it created the cleaner seams the final session built on.
story_review.summary: A coherent, well-tested five-session build that progresses cleanly from a bare WebSocket core to a distributed, persisted, hardened notification service — held back only by a persistent single-file monolith and a partially-applied transport abstraction.
